q: Which term matches this definition? “a contractual provision that wage increases will keep up with inflation”
why: cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs): a contractual provision that wage increases will keep up with inflation

q: Which term matches this definition? “a price, wage, or interest rate is adjusted automatically for inflation”
why: indexed: a price, wage, or interest rate is adjusted automatically for inflation

card.q: How should an increase in inflation affect the interest rate on an adjustable-rate mortgage?
card.a: Higher inflation reduces real interest rates on fixed rate mortgages. Because ARMs can be adjusted, higher inflation leads to higher interest rates on ARMs.

card.q: A fixed-rate mortgage has the same interest rate over the life of the loan, whether the mortgage is for 15 or 30 years. By contrast, an adjustable-rate mortgage changes with market interest rates over the life of the mortgage. If inflation falls unexpectedly by 3%, what would likely happen to a homeowner with an adjustable-rate mortgage?
card.a: Because the mortgage has an adjustable rate, the rate should fall by 3%, the same as inflation, to keep the real interest rate the same.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the gap, if any, between a nation’s exports and imports”
why: balance of trade (trade balance): the gap, if any, between a nation’s exports and imports

q: Which term matches this definition? “a broad measure of the balance of trade that includes trade in goods and services, as well as international flows of income and foreign aid”
why: current account balance: a broad measure of the balance of trade that includes trade in goods and services, as well as international flows of income and foreign aid

q: Which term matches this definition? “the balance of trade looking only at goods”
why: merchandise trade balance: the balance of trade looking only at goods

q: Which term matches this definition? ““one-way payments” that governments, private entities, or individuals make that they sent abroad with nothing received in return”
why: unilateral transfers: “one-way payments” that governments, private entities, or individuals make that they sent abroad with nothing received in return

card.q: If foreign investors buy more U.S. stocks and bonds, how would that show up in the current account balance?
card.a: The stock and bond values will not show up in the current account. However, the dividends from the stocks and the interest from the bonds show up as an import to income in the current account.

card.q: If the trade deficit of the United States increases, how is the current account balance affected?
card.a: It becomes more negative as imports, which are a negative to the current account, are growing faster than exports, which are a positive.

card.q: State whether each of the following events involves a financial flow to the Mexican economy or a financial flow out of the Mexican economy: 1. Mexico imports services from Japan; 2. Mexico exports goods to Canada; 3. U.S. investors receive a return from past financial investments in Mexico
card.a: 1. Money flows out of the Mexican economy.; 2. Money flows into the Mexican economy.; 3. Money flows out of the Mexican economy.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the dollar value of exports divided by the dollar value of a country’s GDP”
options: exports of goods and services as a percentage of GDP
why: exports of goods and services as a percentage of GDP: the dollar value of exports divided by the dollar value of a country’s GDP

card.q: In what way does comparing a country’s exports to GDP reflect its degree of globalization?
card.a: GDP is a dollar value of all production of goods and services. Exports are produced domestically but shipped abroad. The percent ratio of exports to GDP gives us an idea of how important exports are to the national economy out of all goods and services produced. For example, exports represent only 14% of U.S. GDP, but 50% of Germany’s GDP

card.q: At one point Canada’s GDP was $1,800 billion and its exports were $542 billion. What was Canada’s export ratio at this time?
card.a: Divide $542 billion by $1,800 billion.

card.q: The GDP for the United States is $18,036 billion and its current account balance is –$484 billion. What percent of GDP is the current account balance?
card.a: Divide –$400 billion by $16,800 billion.

card.q: Why does the trade balance and the current account balance track so closely together over time?
card.a: The trade balance is the difference between exports and imports. The current account balance includes this number (whether it is a trade balance or a trade surplus), but also includes international flows of money from global investments.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the international flows of money that facilitates trade and investment”
why: financial capital: the international flows of money that facilitates trade and investment

card.q: State whether each of the following events involves a financial flow to the U.S. economy or away from the U.S. economy: 1. Export sales to Germany; 2. Returns paid on past U.S. financial investments in Brazil; 3. Foreign aid from the U.S. government to Egypt; 4. Imported oil from the Russian Federation; 5. Japanese investors buying U.S. real estate
card.a: 1. An export sale to Germany involves a financial flow from Germany to the U.S. economy.; 2. The issue here is not U.S. investments in Brazil, but the return paid on those investments, which involves a financial flow from the Brazilian economy to the U.S. economy.; 3. Foreign aid from the United States to Egypt is a financial flow from the United States to Egypt.; 4. Importing oil from the Russian Federation means a flow of financial payments from the U.S. economy to the Russian Federation.; 5. Japanese investors buying U.S. real estate is a financial flow from Japan to the U.S. economy.

card.q: How does the bottom portion of, showing the international flow of investments and capital, differ from the upper portion?
card.a: The top portion tracks the flow of exports and imports and the payments for those. The bottom portion is looking at international financial investments and the outflow and inflow of monies from those investments. These investments can include investments in stocks and bonds or real estate abroad, as well as international borrowing and lending.

card.q: Explain the relationship between a current account deficit or surplus and the flow of funds.
card.a: If more monies are flowing out of the country (for example, to pay for imports) it will make the current account more negative or less positive, and if more monies are flowing into the country, it will make the current account less negative or more positive.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the total of private savings and public savings (a government budget surplus)”
why: national savings and investment identity: the total of private savings and public savings (a government budget surplus)

card.q: If a country is running a government budget surplus, why is (T – G) on the left side of the saving-investment identity?
card.a: The government is saving rather than borrowing. The supply of savings, whether private or public, is on the left side of the identity.

card.q: What determines the size of a country’s trade deficit?
card.a: A trade deficit is determined by a country’s level of private and public savings and the amount of domestic investment.

card.q: If domestic investment increases, and there is no change in the amount of private and public saving, what must happen to the size of the trade deficit?
card.a: The trade deficit must increase. To put it another way, this increase in investment must be financed by an inflow of financial capital from abroad.

card.q: Why does a recession cause a trade deficit to increase?
card.a: Incomes fall during a recession, and consumers buy fewer good, including imports.

card.q: Both the United States and global economies are booming. Will U.S. imports and/or exports increase?
card.a: A booming economy will increase the demand for goods in general, so import sales will increase. If our trading partners’ economies are doing well, they will buy more of our products and so U.S. exports will increase.

card.q: For each of the following, indicate which type of government spending would justify a budget deficit and which would not. 1. Increased federal spending on Medicare; 2. Increased spending on education; 3. Increased spending on the space program; 4. Increased spending on airports and air traffic control
card.a: 1. Increased federal spending on Medicare may not increase productivity, so a budget deficit is not justified.; 2. Increased spending on education will increase productivity and foster greater economic growth, so a budget deficit is justified.; 3. Increased spending on the space program may not increase productivity, so a budget deficit is not justified.; 4. Increased spending on airports and air traffic control will increase productivity and foster greater economic growth, so a budget deficit is justified.

card.q: How did large trade deficits hurt the East Asian countries in the mid 1980s? (Recall that trade deficits are equivalent to inflows of financial capital from abroad.)
card.a: Foreign investors worried about repayment so they began to pull money out of these countries. The money can be pulled out of stock and bond markets, real estate, and banks.

card.q: Describe a scenario in which a trade surplus benefits an economy and one in which a trade surplus is occurring in an economy that performs poorly. What key factor or factors are making the difference in the outcome that results from a trade surplus?
card.a: A rapidly growing trade surplus could result from a number of factors, so you would not want to be too quick to assume a specific cause. However, if the choice is between whether the economy is in recession or growing rapidly, the answer would have to be recession. In a recession, demand for all goods, including imports, has declined; however, demand for exports from other countries has not necessarily altered much, so the result is a larger trade surplus.

card.q: The United States exports 14% of GDP while Germany exports about 50% of its GDP. Explain what that means.
card.a: Germany has a higher level of trade than the United States. The United States has a large domestic economy so it has a large volume of internal trade.

q: Which term matches this definition? ““demand creates its own supply””
why: Keynes’ law: “demand creates its own supply”

q: Which term matches this definition? “economists who generally emphasize the importance of aggregate supply in determining the size of the macroeconomy over the long run”
why: neoclassical economists: economists who generally emphasize the importance of aggregate supply in determining the size of the macroeconomy over the long run

q: Which term matches this definition? ““supply creates its own demand””
why: Say’s law: “supply creates its own demand”

card.q: Describe the mechanism by which supply creates its own demand.
card.a: In order to supply goods, suppliers must employ workers, whose incomes increase as a result of their labor. They use this additional income to demand goods of an equivalent value to those they supply.

card.q: Describe the mechanism by which demand creates its own supply.
card.a: When consumers demand more goods than are available on the market, prices are driven higher and the additional opportunities for profit induce more suppliers to enter the market, producing an equivalent amount to that which is demanded.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the amount of total spending on domestic goods and services in an economy”
why: aggregate demand (AD): the amount of total spending on domestic goods and services in an economy

q: Which term matches this definition? “the total quantity of output (i.e. real GDP) firms will produce and sell”
why: aggregate supply (AS): the total quantity of output (i.e. real GDP) firms will produce and sell

q: Which term matches this definition? “the total spending on domestic goods and services at each price level”
why: aggregate demand (AD) curve: the total spending on domestic goods and services at each price level

q: Which term matches this definition? “the total quantity of output (i.e. real GDP) that firms will produce and sell at each price level”
why: aggregate supply (AS) curve: the total quantity of output (i.e. real GDP) that firms will produce and sell at each price level

q: Which term matches this definition? “a model that shows what determines total supply or total demand for the economy, and how total demand and total supply interact at the macroeconomic level”
why: aggregate demand/aggregate supply model: a model that shows what determines total supply or total demand for the economy, and how total demand and total supply interact at the macroeconomic level

q: Which term matches this definition? “another name for potential GDP, when the economy is producing at its potential and unemployment is at the natural rate of unemployment”
why: full-employment GDP: another name for potential GDP, when the economy is producing at its potential and unemployment is at the natural rate of unemployment

card.q: The short run aggregate supply curve was constructed assuming that as the price of outputs increases, the price of inputs stays the same. How would an increase in the prices of important inputs, like energy, affect aggregate supply?
card.a: Higher input prices make output less profitable, decreasing the desired supply. This is shown graphically as a leftward shift in the AS curve.

card.q: In the AD/AS model, what prevents the economy from achieving equilibrium at potential output?
card.a: Equilibrium occurs at the level of GDP where AD = AS. Insufficient aggregate demand could explain why the equilibrium occurs at a level of GDP less than potential. A decrease (or leftward shift) in aggregate supply could be another reason.

q: Which term matches this definition? “an economy experiences stagnant growth and high inflation at the same time”
why: stagflation: an economy experiences stagnant growth and high inflation at the same time

card.q: Suppose the U.S. Congress passes significant immigration reform that makes it more difficult for foreigners to come to the United States to work. Use the AD/AS model to explain how this would affect the equilibrium level of GDP and the price level.
card.a: Equilibrium real GDP will decrease and the price level will increase.

card.q: Suppose concerns about the size of the federal budget deficit lead the U.S. Congress to cut all funding for research and development for ten years. Assuming this has an impact on technology growth, what does the AD/AS model predict would be the likely effect on equilibrium GDP and the price level?
card.a: Given the assumptions made here, the cuts in R&D funding should reduce productivity growth. The model would show this as a leftward shift in the SRAS curve, leading to a lower equilibrium GDP and a higher price level.

card.q: How would a dramatic increase in the value of the stock market shift the AD curve? What effect would the shift have on the equilibrium level of GDP and the price level?
card.a: An increase in the value of the stock market would make individuals feel wealthier and thus more confident about their economic situation. This would likely cause an increase in consumer confidence leading to an increase in consumer spending, shifting the AD curve to the right. The result would be an increase in the equilibrium level of GDP and an increase in the price level.

card.q: Suppose Mexico, one of our largest trading partners and purchaser of a large quantity of our exports, goes into a recession. Use the AD/AS model to determine the likely impact on our equilibrium GDP and price level.
card.a: Since imports depend on GDP, if Mexico goes into recession, its GDP declines and so do its imports. This decline in our exports can be shown as a leftward shift in AD, leading to a decrease in our GDP and price level.

card.q: A policymaker claims that tax cuts led the economy out of a recession. Can we use the AD/AS diagram to show this?
card.a: Tax cuts increase consumer and investment spending, depending on where the tax cuts are targeted. This would shift AD to the right, so if the tax cuts occurred when the economy was in recession (and GDP was less than potential), the tax cuts would increase GDP and “lead the economy out of recession.”

card.q: Many financial analysts and economists eagerly await the press releases for the reports on the home price index and consumer confidence index. What would be the effects of a negative report on both of these? What about a positive report?
card.a: A negative report on home prices would make consumers feel like the value of their homes, which for most Americans is a major portion of their wealth, has declined. A negative report on consumer confidence would make consumers feel pessimistic about the future. Both of these would likely reduce consumer spending, shifting AD to the left, reducing GDP and the price level. A positive report on the home price index or consumer confidence would do the opposite.

card.q: What impact would a decrease in the size of the labor force have on GDP and the price level according to the AD/AS model?
card.a: A smaller labor force would be reflected in a leftward shift in AS, leading to a lower equilibrium level of GDP and higher price level.

card.q: Suppose, after five years of sluggish growth, the European Union's economy picks up speed. What would be the likely impact on the U.S. trade balance, GDP, and employment?
card.a: Higher EU growth would increase demand for U.S. exports, reducing our trade deficit. The increased demand for exports would show up as a rightward shift in AD, causing GDP to rise (and the price level to rise as well). Higher GDP would require more jobs to fulfill, so U.S. employment would also rise.

card.q: Suppose the Federal Reserve begins to increase the supply of money at an increasing rate. What impact would that have on GDP, unemployment, and inflation?
card.a: Expansionary monetary policy shifts AD to the right. A continuing expansionary policy would cause larger and larger shifts (given the parameters of this problem). The result would be an increase in GDP and employment (a decrease in unemployment) and higher prices until potential output was reached. After that point, the expansionary policy would simply cause inflation.

q: Which term matches this definition? “portion of the SRAS curve where GDP is below potential but not so far below as in the Keynesian zone; the SRAS curve is upward-sloping, but not vertical in the intermediate zone”
why: intermediate zone: portion of the SRAS curve where GDP is below potential but not so far below as in the Keynesian zone; the SRAS curve is upward-sloping, but not vertical in the intermediate zone

q: Which term matches this definition? “portion of the SRAS curve where GDP is far below potential and the SRAS curve is flat”
why: Keynesian zone: portion of the SRAS curve where GDP is far below potential and the SRAS curve is flat

q: Which term matches this definition? “portion of the SRAS curve where GDP is at or near potential output where the SRAS curve is steep”
why: neoclassical zone: portion of the SRAS curve where GDP is at or near potential output where the SRAS curve is steep

card.q: If the economy is operating in the neoclassical zone of the SRAS curve and aggregate demand falls, what is likely to happen to real GDP?
card.a: Since the SRAS curve is vertical in the neoclassical zone, unless the economy is bordering the intermediate zone, a decrease in AS will cause a decrease in the price level, but no effect on real economic activity (for example, real GDP or employment).

card.q: If the economy is operating in the Keynesian zone of the SRAS curve and aggregate demand falls, what is likely to happen to real GDP?
card.a: Because the SRAS curve is horizontal in the Keynesian zone, a decrease in AD should depress real economic activity but have no effect on prices.

q: Which term matches this definition? “equilibrium at a level of output above potential GDP”
why: inflationary gap: equilibrium at a level of output above potential GDP

q: Which term matches this definition? “the amount of goods and services actually sold in a nation”
why: real GDP: the amount of goods and services actually sold in a nation

q: Which term matches this definition? “equilibrium at a level of output below potential GDP”
why: recessionary gap: equilibrium at a level of output below potential GDP

card.q: In the Keynesian framework, which of the following events might cause a recession? Which might cause inflation? Sketch AD/AS diagrams to illustrate your answers. 1. A large increase in the price of the homes people own.; 2. Rapid growth in the economy of a major trading partner.; 3. Business confidence increases.; 4. The interest rate rises.; 5. The good imported from a major trading partner become much less expensive.
card.a: 1. An increase in home values will increase consumption spending (due to increased wealth). AD will shift to the right and may cause inflation if it goes beyond potential GDP.; 2. Rapid growth by a major trading partner will increase demand for exports. AD will shift to the right and may cause inflation if it goes beyond potential GDP.; 3. Increased profit opportunities will increase business investment. AD will shift to the right and may cause inflation if it goes beyond potential GDP.; 4. Higher interest rates reduce investment spending. AD will shift to the left and may cause recession if it falls below potential GDP.; 5. Demand for cheaper imports increases, reducing demand for domestic products. AD will shift to the left and may be recessionary.

q: Which term matches this definition? “downward wage and price flexibility requires perfect information about the level of lower compensation acceptable to other laborers and market participants”
why: coordination argument: downward wage and price flexibility requires perfect information about the level of lower compensation acceptable to other laborers and market participants

q: Which term matches this definition? “Keynesian concept that asserts that a change in autonomous spending causes a more than proportionate change in real GDP”
why: expenditure multiplier: Keynesian concept that asserts that a change in autonomous spending causes a more than proportionate change in real GDP

q: Which term matches this definition? “costs firms face in changing prices”
why: menu costs: costs firms face in changing prices

q: Which term matches this definition? “a situation where wages and prices do not fall in response to a decrease in demand, or do not rise in response to an increase in demand”
why: sticky wages and prices: a situation where wages and prices do not fall in response to a decrease in demand, or do not rise in response to an increase in demand

card.q: Use the AD/AS model to explain how an inflationary gap occurs, beginning from the initial equilibrium in.
card.a: An inflationary gap is the result of an increase in aggregate demand when the economy is at potential output. Since the AS curve is vertical at potential GDP, any increase in AD will lead to a higher price level (i.e. inflation) but no higher real GDP. This is easy to see if you draw AD₁ to the right of AD₀.

card.q: Suppose the U.S. Congress cuts federal government spending in order to balance the Federal budget. Use the AD/AS model to analyze the likely impact on output and employment. Hint: revisit.
card.a: A decrease in government spending will shift AD to the left.

q: Which term matches this definition? “tax increases or cuts in government spending designed to decrease aggregate demand and reduce inflationary pressures”
why: contractionary fiscal policy: tax increases or cuts in government spending designed to decrease aggregate demand and reduce inflationary pressures

q: Which term matches this definition? “tax cuts or increases in government spending designed to stimulate aggregate demand and move the economy out of recession”
why: expansionary fiscal policy: tax cuts or increases in government spending designed to stimulate aggregate demand and move the economy out of recession

q: Which term matches this definition? “the tradeoff between unemployment and inflation”
why: Phillips curve: the tradeoff between unemployment and inflation

card.q: How would a decrease in energy prices affect the Phillips curve?
card.a: A decrease in energy prices, a positive supply shock, would cause the AS curve to shift out to the right, yielding more real GDP at a lower price level. This would shift the Phillips curve down toward the origin, meaning the economy would experience lower unemployment and a lower rate of inflation.

card.q: Does Keynesian economics require government to set controls on prices, wages, or interest rates?
card.a: Keynesian economics does not require microeconomic price controls of any sort. It is true that many Keynesian economic prescriptions were for the government to influence the total amount of aggregate demand in the economy, often through government spending and tax cuts.

card.q: List three practical problems with the Keynesian perspective.
card.a: The three problems center on government’s ability to estimate potential GDP, decide whether to influence aggregate demand through tax changes or changes in government spending, and the lag time that occurs as Congress and the President attempt to pass legislation.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the theory that people look at past experience and gradually adapt their beliefs and behavior as circumstances change”
why: adaptive expectations: the theory that people look at past experience and gradually adapt their beliefs and behavior as circumstances change

q: Which term matches this definition? “the philosophy that, in the long run, the business cycle will fluctuate around the potential, or full-employment, level of output”
why: neoclassical perspective: the philosophy that, in the long run, the business cycle will fluctuate around the potential, or full-employment, level of output

q: Which term matches this definition? “the amount and kind of machinery and equipment available to help a person produce a good or service”
why: physical capital per person: the amount and kind of machinery and equipment available to help a person produce a good or service

q: Which term matches this definition? “the theory that people form the most accurate possible expectations about the future that they can, using all information available to them”
options: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)
why: rational expectations: the theory that people form the most accurate possible expectations about the future that they can, using all information available to them

card.q: Do rational expectations tend to look back at past experience while adaptive expectations look ahead to the future? Explain your answer.
card.a: No, this statement is false. It would be more accurate to say that rational expectations seek to predict the future as accurately as possible, using all of past experience as a guide. Adaptive expectations are largely backward looking; that is, they adapt as experience accumulates, but without attempting to look forward.

q: Which term matches this definition? “a future rate of inflation that consumers and firms build into current decision making”
why: expected inflation: a future rate of inflation that consumers and firms build into current decision making

card.q: Would it make sense to argue that rational expectations economics is an extreme version of neoclassical economics? Explain.
card.a: The statement is accurate. Rational expectations can be thought of as a version of neoclassical economics because it argues that potential GDP and the rate of unemployment are shaped by market forces as wages and prices adjust. However, it is an “extreme” version because it argues that this adjustment takes place very quickly. Other theories, like adaptive expectations, suggest that adjustment to the neoclassical outcome takes a few years.

card.q: Summarize the Keynesian and Neoclassical models.
card.a: The short-term Keynesian model is built on the importance of aggregate demand as a cause of business cycles and a degree of wage and price rigidity, and thus does a sound job of explaining many recessions and why cyclical unemployment rises and falls. The neoclassical model emphasizes aggregate supply by focusing on the underlying determinants of output and employment in markets, and thus tends to put more emphasis on economic growth and how labor markets work.

q: Which term matches this definition? “literally, trading one good or service for another, without using money”
why: barter: literally, trading one good or service for another, without using money

q: Which term matches this definition? “an item that is used as money, but which also has value from its use as something other than money”
why: commodity money: an item that is used as money, but which also has value from its use as something other than money

q: Which term matches this definition? “dollar bills or other currencies with values backed up by gold or another commodity”
why: commodity-backed currencies: dollar bills or other currencies with values backed up by gold or another commodity

q: Which term matches this definition? “a situation in which two people each want some good or service that the other person can provide”

q: Which term matches this definition? “has no intrinsic value, but is declared by a government to be the country's legal tender”

q: Which term matches this definition? “whatever is widely accepted as a method of payment”
why: medium of exchange: whatever is widely accepted as a method of payment

card.q: In many casinos, a person buys chips to use for gambling. Within the casino's walls, customers often can use these chips to buy food and drink or even a hotel room. Do chips in a gambling casino serve all three functions of money?
card.a: As long as you remain within the walls of the casino, chips fit the definition of money; that is, they serve as a medium of exchange, a unit of account, and a store of value. Chips do not work very well as money once you leave the casino, but many kinds of money do not work well in other areas. For example, it is hard to spend money from Turkey or Brazil at your local supermarket or at the movie theater.

card.q: Can you name some item that is a store of value, but does not serve the other functions of money?
card.a: Many physical items that a person buys at one time but may sell at another time can serve as an answer to this question. Examples include a house, land, art, rare coins or stamps, and so on.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the coins and bills that circulate in an economy that are not held by the U.S Treasury, at the Federal Reserve Bank, or in bank vaults”
why: coins and currency in circulation: the coins and bills that circulate in an economy that are not held by the U.S Treasury, at the Federal Reserve Bank, or in bank vaults

q: Which term matches this definition? “immediately transfers money from the credit card company’s checking account to the seller, and at the end of the month the user owes the money to the credit card company; a credit card is a short-term loan”
why: credit card: immediately transfers money from the credit card company’s checking account to the seller, and at the end of the month the user owes the money to the credit card company; a credit card is a short-term loan

q: Which term matches this definition? “like a check, is an instruction to the user’s bank to transfer money directly and immediately from your bank account to the seller”
why: debit card: like a check, is an instruction to the user’s bank to transfer money directly and immediately from your bank account to the seller

q: Which term matches this definition? “checkable deposit in banks that is available by making a cash withdrawal or writing a check”
why: demand deposit: checkable deposit in banks that is available by making a cash withdrawal or writing a check

q: Which term matches this definition? “a definition of the money supply that includes currency in circulation, checking and savings accounts in banks, and to a lesser degree, traveler’s checks.”
why: M1 money supply: a definition of the money supply that includes currency in circulation, checking and savings accounts in banks, and to a lesser degree, traveler’s checks.

q: Which term matches this definition? “a broad definition of the money supply that includes everything in M1, but also adds money market funds and certificates of deposit”
why: M2 money supply: a broad definition of the money supply that includes everything in M1, but also adds money market funds and certificates of deposit

card.q: If you are out shopping for clothes and books, what is easiest and most convenient for you to spend: M1 or M2? Explain your answer.
card.a: The currency and checks in M1 are easiest to spend. It is harder to spend M2 directly, although if there is an automatic teller machine in the shopping mall, you can turn M2 from your savings account into an M1 of currency quite quickly. If your answer is about “credit cards,” then you are really talking about spending M1—although it is M1 from the account of the credit card company, which you will repay later when you credit card bill comes due.

card.q: For the following list of items, indicate if they are in M1, M2, or neither: 1. Your $5,000 line of credit on your Bank of America card; 2. $50 dollars’ worth of traveler’s checks you have not used yet; 3. $1 in quarters in your pocket; 4. $1200 in your checking account; 5. $2000 you have in a money market account
card.a: 1. Neither in M1 or M2; 2. That is part of M1, and because M2 includes M1 it is also part of M2; 3. Currency out in the public hands is part of M1 and M2; 4. Checking deposits are in M1 and M2; 5. Money market accounts are in M2

q: Which term matches this definition? “when banks are holding an amount of reserves significantly above the minimum required amount; generally a choice made by banks during and after the Great Recession”
why: ample reserves: when banks are holding an amount of reserves significantly above the minimum required amount; generally a choice made by banks during and after the Great Recession
