why: balance sheet: an accounting tool that lists assets and liabilities

q: Which term matches this definition? “institution that accepts money deposits and then uses these to make loans”
why: depository institution: institution that accepts money deposits and then uses these to make loans

q: Which term matches this definition? “making loans or investments with a variety of firms, to reduce the risk of being adversely affected by events at one or a few firms”
why: diversify: making loans or investments with a variety of firms, to reduce the risk of being adversely affected by events at one or a few firms

card.q: Explain why the money listed under assets on a bank balance sheet may not actually be in the bank?
card.a: A bank’s assets include cash held in their vaults, but assets also include monies that the bank holds at the Federal Reserve Bank (called “reserves”), loans that are made to customers, and bonds.

q: Which term matches this definition? “formula used to determine the total amount of M1 money supply created in the banking system; equal to 1/reserve ratio”
why: money multiplier formula: formula used to determine the total amount of M1 money supply created in the banking system; equal to 1/reserve ratio

q: Which term matches this definition? “institution which conducts a nation’s monetary policy and regulates its banking system”
why: central bank: institution which conducts a nation’s monetary policy and regulates its banking system

card.q: Why is it important for the members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve to have longer terms in office than elected officials, like the President?
card.a: Longer terms insulate the Board from political forces. Since the presidency can potentially change every four years, the Federal Reserve’s independence prevents drastic swings in monetary policy with every new administration and allows policy decisions to be made only on economic grounds.

q: Which term matches this definition? “when depositors race to the bank to withdraw their deposits for fear that otherwise they would be lost”
why: bank run: when depositors race to the bank to withdraw their deposits for fear that otherwise they would be lost

q: Which term matches this definition? “an insurance system that makes sure depositors in a bank do not lose their money, even if the bank goes bankrupt”
why: deposit insurance: an insurance system that makes sure depositors in a bank do not lose their money, even if the bank goes bankrupt

q: Which term matches this definition? “an institution that provides short-term emergency loans in conditions of financial crisis”
why: lender of last resort: an institution that provides short-term emergency loans in conditions of financial crisis

card.q: Given the danger of bank runs, why do banks not keep the majority of deposits on hand to meet the demands of depositors?
card.a: Banks make their money from issuing loans and charging interest. The more money that is stored in the bank’s vault, the less is available for lending and the less money the bank stands to make.

card.q: Bank runs are often described as “self-fulfilling prophecies.” Why is this phrase appropriate to bank runs?
card.a: The fear and uncertainty created by the suggestion that a bank might fail can lead depositors to withdraw their money. If many depositors do this at the same time, the bank may not be able to meet their demands and will, indeed, fail.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the interest rate charged by the central bank on the loans that it gives to other commercial banks”
why: discount rate: the interest rate charged by the central bank on the loans that it gives to other commercial banks

q: Which term matches this definition? “the central bank selling or buying Treasury bonds to influence the quantity of money and the level of interest rates”
why: open market operations: the central bank selling or buying Treasury bonds to influence the quantity of money and the level of interest rates

q: Which term matches this definition? “the percentage amount of its total deposits that a bank is legally obligated to either hold as cash in their vault or deposit with the central bank”
why: reserve requirement: the percentage amount of its total deposits that a bank is legally obligated to either hold as cash in their vault or deposit with the central bank

card.q: If the central bank sells $500 in bonds to a bank that has issued $10,000 in loans and is exactly meeting the reserve requirement of 10%, what will happen to the amount of loans and to the money supply in general?
card.a: The bank has to hold $1,000 in reserves, so when it buys the $500 in bonds, it will have to reduce its loans by $500 to make up the difference. The money supply decreases by the same amount.

card.q: What would be the effect of increasing the banks' reserve requirements on the money supply?
card.a: An increase in reserve requirements would reduce the supply of money, since more money would be held in banks rather than circulating in the economy.

q: Which term matches this definition? “a monetary policy that reduces the supply of money and loans”
why: contractionary monetary policy: a monetary policy that reduces the supply of money and loans

q: Which term matches this definition? “moving in the opposite direction of the business cycle of economic downturns and upswings”
why: countercyclical: moving in the opposite direction of the business cycle of economic downturns and upswings

q: Which term matches this definition? “a monetary policy that increases the supply of money and the quantity of loans”
why: expansionary monetary policy: a monetary policy that increases the supply of money and the quantity of loans

q: Which term matches this definition? “the interest rate at which one bank lends funds to another bank overnight”
why: federal funds rate: the interest rate at which one bank lends funds to another bank overnight

q: Which term matches this definition? “see expansionary monetary policy”
why: loose monetary policy: see expansionary monetary policy

q: Which term matches this definition? “the purchase of long term government and private mortgage-backed securities by central banks to make credit available in hopes of stimulating aggregate demand”
why: quantitative easing (QE): the purchase of long term government and private mortgage-backed securities by central banks to make credit available in hopes of stimulating aggregate demand

card.q: Why does contractionary monetary policy cause interest rates to rise?
card.a: Contractionary policy reduces the amount of loanable funds in the economy. As with all goods, greater scarcity leads a greater price, so the interest rate, or the price of borrowing money, rises.

card.q: Why does expansionary monetary policy causes interest rates to drop?
card.a: An increase in the amount of available loanable funds means that there are more people who want to lend. They, therefore, bid the price of borrowing (the interest rate) down.

q: Which term matches this definition? “money supply × velocity = nominal GDP”
why: basic quantity equation of money: money supply × velocity = nominal GDP

q: Which term matches this definition? “reserves banks hold that exceed the legally mandated limit”
why: excess reserves: reserves banks hold that exceed the legally mandated limit

q: Which term matches this definition? “a rule that the central bank is required to focus only on keeping inflation low”
why: inflation targeting: a rule that the central bank is required to focus only on keeping inflation low

q: Which term matches this definition? “the interest the Federal Reserve pays banks on their reserves held at their Federal Reserve bank”
why: interest rate on reserve balances (IORB): the interest the Federal Reserve pays banks on their reserves held at their Federal Reserve bank

q: Which term matches this definition? “the speed with which money circulates through the economy; calculated as the nominal GDP divided by the money supply”
why: velocity: the speed with which money circulates through the economy; calculated as the nominal GDP divided by the money supply

card.q: Why might banks want to hold excess reserves in time of recession?
card.a: In times of economic uncertainty, banks may worry that borrowers will lose the ability to repay their loans. They may also fear that a panic is more likely and they will need the excess reserves to meet their obligations.

card.q: Why might the velocity of money change unexpectedly?
card.a: If consumer optimism changes, spending can speed up or slow down. This could also happen in a case where consumers need to buy a large number of items quickly, such as in a situation of national emergency.

q: Which term matches this definition? “when a currency is worth more in terms of other currencies; also called “strengthening””
why: appreciating: when a currency is worth more in terms of other currencies; also called “strengthening”

q: Which term matches this definition? “when a currency is worth less in terms of other currencies; also called “weakening””
why: depreciating: when a currency is worth less in terms of other currencies; also called “weakening”

q: Which term matches this definition? “a country that is not the United States uses the U.S. dollar as its currency”
why: dollarize: a country that is not the United States uses the U.S. dollar as its currency

q: Which term matches this definition? “purchasing more than ten percent of a firm or starting a new enterprise in another country”
why: foreign direct investment (FDI): purchasing more than ten percent of a firm or starting a new enterprise in another country

q: Which term matches this definition? “the market in which people use one currency to buy another currency”
why: foreign exchange market: the market in which people use one currency to buy another currency

q: Which term matches this definition? “using a financial transaction as protection against risk”
why: hedge: using a financial transaction as protection against risk

q: Which term matches this definition? “the process of buying a good and selling goods across borders to take advantage of international price differences”
why: arbitrage: the process of buying a good and selling goods across borders to take advantage of international price differences

q: Which term matches this definition? “the exchange rate that equalizes the prices of internationally traded goods across countries”
why: purchasing power parity (PPP): the exchange rate that equalizes the prices of internationally traded goods across countries

card.q: Suppose that political unrest in Egypt leads financial markets to anticipate a depreciation in the Egyptian pound. How will that affect the demand for pounds, supply of pounds, and exchange rate for pounds compared to, say, U.S. dollars?
card.a: Expected depreciation in a currency will lead people to divest themselves of the currency. We should expect to see an increase in the supply of pounds and a decrease in demand for pounds. The result should be a decrease in the value of the pound vis à vis the dollar.

card.q: Suppose U.S. interest rates decline compared to the rest of the world. What would be the likely impact on the demand for dollars, supply of dollars, and exchange rate for dollars compared to, say, euros?
card.a: Lower U.S. interest rates make U.S. assets less desirable compared to assets in the European Union. We should expect to see a decrease in demand for dollars and an increase in supply of dollars in foreign currency markets. As a result, we should expect to see the dollar depreciate compared to the euro.

card.q: Suppose Argentina gets inflation under control and the Argentine inflation rate decreases substantially. What would likely happen to the demand for Argentine pesos, the supply of Argentine pesos, and the peso/U.S. dollar exchange rate?
card.a: A decrease in Argentine inflation relative to other countries should cause an increase in demand for pesos, a decrease in supply of pesos, and an appreciation of the peso in foreign currency markets.

card.q: This chapter has explained that “one of the most economically destructive effects of exchange rate fluctuations can happen through the banking system,” if banks borrow from abroad to lend domestically. Why is this less likely to be a problem for the U.S. banking system?
card.a: The problem occurs when banks borrow foreign currency but lend in domestic currency. Since banks’ assets (loans they made) are in domestic currency, while their debts (money they borrowed) are in foreign currency, when the domestic currency declines, their debts grow larger. If the domestic currency falls substantially in value, as happened during the Asian financial crisis, then the banking system could fail. This problem is unlikely to occur for U.S. banks because, even when they borrow from abroad, they tend to borrow dollars. Remember, there are trillions of dollars in circulation in the global economy. Since both assets and debts are in dollars, a change in the value of the dollar does not cause banking system failure the way it can when banks borrow in foreign currency.

card.q: A booming economy can attract financial capital inflows, which promote further growth. However, capital can just as easily flow out of the country, leading to economic recession. Is a country whose economy is booming because it decided to stimulate consumer spending more or less likely to experience capital flight than an economy whose boom is caused by economic investment expenditure?
card.a: While capital flight is possible in either case, if a country borrows to invest in real capital it is more likely to be able to generate the income to pay back its debts than a country that borrows to finance consumption. As a result, an investment-stimulated economy is less likely to provoke capital flight and economic recession.

q: Which term matches this definition? “a country lets the exchange rate market determine its currency's value”
why: floating exchange rate: a country lets the exchange rate market determine its currency's value

q: Which term matches this definition? “an exchange rate policy in which the central bank sets a fixed and unchanging value for the exchange rate”
why: hard peg: an exchange rate policy in which the central bank sets a fixed and unchanging value for the exchange rate

q: Which term matches this definition? “flow of financial capital across national boundaries either as portfolio investment or direct investment”
why: international capital flows: flow of financial capital across national boundaries either as portfolio investment or direct investment

q: Which term matches this definition? “when a nation chooses to use another nation's currency”
why: merged currency: when a nation chooses to use another nation's currency

q: Which term matches this definition? “an exchange rate policy in which the government usually allows the market to set the exchange rate, but in some cases, especially if the exchange rate seems to be moving rapidly in one direction, the central bank will intervene”
why: soft peg: an exchange rate policy in which the government usually allows the market to set the exchange rate, but in some cases, especially if the exchange rate seems to be moving rapidly in one direction, the central bank will intervene

q: Which term matches this definition? “see international capital flows”
why: Tobin taxes: see international capital flows

card.q: How would a contractionary monetary policy affect the exchange rate, net exports, aggregate demand, and aggregate supply?
card.a: A contractionary monetary policy, by driving up domestic interest rates, would cause the currency to appreciate. The higher value of the currency in foreign exchange markets would reduce exports, since from the perspective of foreign buyers, they are now more expensive. The higher value of the currency would similarly stimulate imports, since they would now be cheaper from the perspective of domestic buyers. Lower exports and higher imports cause net exports (EX – IM) to fall, which causes aggregate demand to fall. The result would be a decrease in GDP working through the exchange rate mechanism reinforcing the effect contractionary monetary policy has on domestic investment expenditure. However, cheaper imports would stimulate aggregate supply, bringing GDP back to potential, though at a lower price level.

card.q: A central bank can allow its currency to fall indefinitely, but it cannot allow its currency to rise indefinitely. Why not?
card.a: For a currency to fall, a central bank need only supply more of its currency in foreign exchange markets. It can print as much domestic currency as it likes. For a currency to rise, a central bank needs to buy its currency in foreign exchange markets, paying with foreign currency. Since no central bank has an infinite amount of foreign currency reserves, it cannot buy its currency indefinitely.

card.q: Is a country for which imports and exports comprise a large fraction of the GDP more likely to adopt a flexible exchange rate or a fixed (hard peg) exchange rate?
card.a: Variations in exchange rates, because they change import and export prices, disturb international trade flows. When trade is a large part of a nation’s economic activity, government will find it more advantageous to fix exchange rates to minimize disruptions of trade flows.

q: Which term matches this definition? “when government spending and taxes are equal”
why: balanced budget: when government spending and taxes are equal

q: Which term matches this definition? “when the federal government spends more money than it receives in taxes in a given year”
why: budget deficit: when the federal government spends more money than it receives in taxes in a given year

q: Which term matches this definition? “when the government receives more money in taxes than it spends in a year”
why: budget surplus: when the government receives more money in taxes than it spends in a year

card.q: When governments run budget deficits, how do they make up the differences between tax revenue and spending?
card.a: The government borrows funds by selling Treasury bonds, notes, and bills.

card.q: When governments run budget surpluses, what is done with the extra funds?
card.a: The funds can be used to pay down the national debt or else be refunded to the taxpayers.

card.q: Is it possible for a nation to run budget deficits and still have its debt/GDP ratio fall? Explain your answer. Is it possible for a nation to run budget surpluses and still have its debt/GDP ratio rise? Explain your answer.
card.a: Yes, a nation can run budget deficits and see its debt/GDP ratio fall. In fact, this is not uncommon. If the deficit is small in a given year, than the addition to debt in the numerator of the debt/GDP ratio will be relatively small, while the growth in GDP is larger, and so the debt/GDP ratio declines. This was the experience of the U.S. economy for the period from the end of World War II to about 1980. It is also theoretically possible, although not likely, for a nation to have a budget surplus and see its debt/GDP ratio rise. Imagine the case of a nation with a small surplus, but in a recession year when the economy shrinks. It is possible that the decline in the nation’s debt, in the numerator of the debt/GDP ratio, would be proportionally less than the fall in the size of GDP, so the debt/GDP ratio would rise.

q: Which term matches this definition? “a tax imposed on corporate profits”
why: corporate income tax: a tax imposed on corporate profits

q: Which term matches this definition? “a tax on people who pass assets to the next generation—either after death or during life in the form of gifts”
why: estate and gift tax: a tax on people who pass assets to the next generation—either after death or during life in the form of gifts

q: Which term matches this definition? “a tax on a specific good—on gasoline, tobacco, and alcohol”
why: excise tax: a tax on a specific good—on gasoline, tobacco, and alcohol

q: Which term matches this definition? “a tax based on the income, of all forms, received by individuals”
why: individual income tax: a tax based on the income, of all forms, received by individuals

q: Which term matches this definition? “or the tax that must be paid on all yearly income”
why: marginal tax rates: or the tax that must be paid on all yearly income

q: Which term matches this definition? “a tax based on the pay received from employers; the taxes provide funds for Social Security and Medicare”
why: payroll tax: a tax based on the pay received from employers; the taxes provide funds for Social Security and Medicare

card.q: Suppose that gifts were taxed at a rate of 10% for amounts up to $100,000 and 20% for anything over that amount. Would this tax be regressive or progressive?
card.a: Progressive. People who give larger gifts subject to the higher tax rate would typically have larger incomes as well.

card.q: If an individual owns a corporation for which he is the only employee, which different types of federal tax will he have to pay?
card.a: Corporate income tax on his profits, individual income tax on his salary, and payroll tax taken out of the wages he pays himself.

card.q: What taxes would an individual pay if he were self-employed and the business is not incorporated?
card.a: individual income taxes

card.q: The social security tax is 6.2% on employees’ income earned below $113,000. Is this tax progressive, regressive or proportional?
card.a: The tax is regressive because wealthy income earners are not taxed at all on income above $113,000. As a percent of total income, the social security tax hits lower income earners harder than wealthier individuals.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the total accumulated amount the government has borrowed, over time, and not yet paid back”
why: national debt: the total accumulated amount the government has borrowed, over time, and not yet paid back

card.q: Debt has a certain self-reinforcing quality to it. There is one category of government spending that automatically increases along with the federal debt. What is it?
card.a: As debt increases, interest payments also rise, so that the deficit grows even if we keep other government spending constant.

q: Which term matches this definition? “fiscal policy that decreases the level of aggregate demand, either through cuts in government spending or increases in taxes”
why: contractionary fiscal policy: fiscal policy that decreases the level of aggregate demand, either through cuts in government spending or increases in taxes

q: Which term matches this definition? “fiscal policy that increases the level of aggregate demand, either through increases in government spending or cuts in taxes”
why: expansionary fiscal policy: fiscal policy that increases the level of aggregate demand, either through increases in government spending or cuts in taxes

card.q: What is the main reason for employing contractionary fiscal policy in a time of strong economic growth?
card.a: To keep prices from rising too much or too rapidly.

card.q: What is the main reason for employing expansionary fiscal policy during a recession?
card.a: To increase employment.

q: Which term matches this definition? “tax and spending rules that have the effect of slowing down the rate of decrease in aggregate demand when the economy slows down and restraining aggregate demand when the economy speeds up, without any additional change in legislation”
why: automatic stabilizers: tax and spending rules that have the effect of slowing down the rate of decrease in aggregate demand when the economy slows down and restraining aggregate demand when the economy speeds up, without any additional change in legislation

q: Which term matches this definition? “the government passes a new law that explicitly changes overall tax or spending levels with the intent of influencing the level of overall economic activity”
why: discretionary fiscal policy: the government passes a new law that explicitly changes overall tax or spending levels with the intent of influencing the level of overall economic activity

q: Which term matches this definition? “the budget deficit or surplus in any given year adjusted for what it would have been if the economy were producing at potential GDP”
why: standardized employment budget: the budget deficit or surplus in any given year adjusted for what it would have been if the economy were producing at potential GDP

card.q: In a recession, does the actual budget surplus or deficit fall above or below the standardized employment budget?
card.a: It falls below because less tax revenue than expected is collected.

card.q: What is the main advantage of automatic stabilizers over discretionary fiscal policy?
card.a: Automatic stabilizers take effect very quickly, whereas discretionary policy can take a long time to implement.

q: Which term matches this definition? “federal spending and borrowing causes interest rates to rise and business investment to fall”
why: crowding out: federal spending and borrowing causes interest rates to rise and business investment to fall

q: Which term matches this definition? “the time it takes for the funds relating to fiscal policy to be dispersed to the appropriate agencies to implement the programs”
why: implementation lag: the time it takes for the funds relating to fiscal policy to be dispersed to the appropriate agencies to implement the programs

q: Which term matches this definition? “the time it takes to get a fiscal policy bill passed”
why: legislative lag: the time it takes to get a fiscal policy bill passed

q: Which term matches this definition? “the time it takes to determine that a recession has occurred”
why: recognition lag: the time it takes to determine that a recession has occurred

card.q: What would happen if expansionary fiscal policy was implemented in a recession but, due to lag, did not actually take effect until after the economy was back to potential GDP?
card.a: Prices would be pushed up as a result of too much spending.

card.q: What would happen if contractionary fiscal policy were implemented during an economic boom but, due to lag, it did not take effect until the economy slipped into recession?
card.a: Employment would suffer as a result of too little spending.

card.q: Do you think the typical time lag for fiscal policy is likely to be longer or shorter than the time lag for monetary policy? Explain your answer?
card.a: Monetary policy probably has shorter time lags than fiscal policy. Imagine that the data becomes fairly clear that an economy is in or near a recession. Expansionary monetary policy can be carried out through open market operations, which can be done fairly quickly, since the Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee meets six times a year. Also, monetary policy takes effect through interest rates, which can change fairly quickly. However, fiscal policy is carried out through acts of Congress that need to be signed into law by the president. Negotiating such laws often takes months, and even after the laws are negotiated, it takes more months for spending programs or tax cuts to have an effect on the macroeconomy.

card.q: How would a balanced budget amendment affect a decision by Congress to grant a tax cut during a recession?
card.a: The government would have to make up the revenue either by raising taxes in a different area or cutting spending.

card.q: How would a balanced budget amendment change the effect of automatic stabilizer programs?
card.a: Programs where the amount of spending is not fixed, but rather determined by macroeconomic conditions, such as food stamps, would lose a great deal of flexibility if spending increases had to be met by corresponding tax increases or spending cuts.

card.q: In a country, private savings equals 600, the government budget surplus equals 200, and the trade surplus equals 100. What is the level of private investment in this economy?
card.a: We use the national savings and investment identity to solve this question. In this case, the government has a budget surplus, so the government surplus appears as part of the supply of financial capital. Then: Quantity supplied of financial capital = Quantity demanded of financial capital; S + (T – G) = I + (X – M); 600 + 200 = I + 100; I = 700

card.q: In the late 1990s, the U.S. government moved from a budget deficit to a budget surplus and the trade deficit in the U.S. economy grew substantially. Using the national saving and investment identity, what can you say about the direction in which saving and/or investment must have changed in this economy?
card.a: In this case, the national saving and investment identity is written in this way: Quantity supplied of financial capital = Quantity demanded of financial capital; (T – G) + (M – X) + S = I The increase in the government budget surplus and the increase in the trade deficit both increased the supply of financial capital. If investment in physical capital remained unchanged, then private savings must go down, and if savings remained unchanged, then investment must go up. In fact, both effects happened; that is, in the late 1990s, in the U.S. economy, savings declined and investment rose.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the theory that rational private households might shift their saving to offset government saving or borrowing”
why: Ricardian equivalence: the theory that rational private households might shift their saving to offset government saving or borrowing

q: Which term matches this definition? “deficits that occur when a country is running both a trade and a budget deficit”
why: twin deficits: deficits that occur when a country is running both a trade and a budget deficit

card.q: Imagine an economy in which Ricardian equivalence holds. This economy has a budget deficit of 50, a trade deficit of 20, private savings of 130, and investment of 100. If the budget deficit rises to 70, how are the other terms in the national saving and investment identity affected?
card.a: Ricardian equivalence means that private saving changes to offset exactly any changes in the government budget. So, if the deficit increases by 20, private saving increases by 20 as well, and the trade deficit and the budget deficit will not change from their original levels. The original national saving and investment identity is written below. Notice that if any change in the (G – T) term is offset by a change in the S term, then the other terms do not change. So if (G – T) rises by 20, then S must also increase by 20. Quantity supplied of financial capital = Quantity demanded of financial capital; S + (M – X) = I + (G – T); 130 + 20 = 100 + 50

q: Which term matches this definition? “a program for early childhood education directed at families with limited educational and financial resources.”
why: Head Start program: a program for early childhood education directed at families with limited educational and financial resources.

card.q: What are some steps the government can take to encourage research and development?
card.a: The government can direct government spending to R&D. It can also create tax incentives for business to invest in R&D.

card.q: What are the drawbacks to analyzing the global economy on a regional basis?
card.a: A region can have some of high-income countries and some of the low-income countries. Aggregating per capita real GDP will vary widely across countries within a region, so aggregating data for a region has little meaning. For example, if you were to compare per capital real GDP for the United States, Canada, Haiti, and Honduras, it looks much different than if you looked at the same data for North America as a whole. Thus, regional comparisons are broad-based and may not adequately capture an individual country’s economic attributes.

q: Which term matches this definition? “a series of studies that show, statistically, that 70% of the differences in income per person across the world is explained by differences in physical capital (savings/investment)”
why: growth consensus: a series of studies that show, statistically, that 70% of the differences in income per person across the world is explained by differences in physical capital (savings/investment)

q: Which term matches this definition? “nation with a per capita income of $12,475 or more; typically has high levels of human and physical capital”
why: high-income country: nation with a per capita income of $12,475 or more; typically has high levels of human and physical capital

q: Which term matches this definition? “a nation that has a per capita income of less than $1,025; a third of the world’s population”
why: low-income country: a nation that has a per capita income of less than $1,025; a third of the world’s population

q: Which term matches this definition? “a nation with per capita income between $1,025 and $12, 475 and that has shown some ability, even if not always sustained, to catch up to the technology leaders in high-income countries”
why: middle-income country: a nation with per capita income between $1,025 and $12, 475 and that has shown some ability, even if not always sustained, to catch up to the technology leaders in high-income countries

card.q: Use the data in the text to contrast the policy prescriptions of the high-income, middle-income, and low-income countries.
card.a: Low-income countries must adopt government policies that are market-oriented and that educate the workforce and population. After this is done, low-income countries should focus on eradicating other social ills that inhibit their growth. The economically challenged are stuck in poverty traps. They need to focus more on health and education and create a stable macroeconomic and political environment. This will attract foreign aid and foreign investment. Middle-income countries strive for increases in physical capital and innovation, while higher-income countries must work to maintain their economies through innovation and technology.

card.q: What are the different policy tools for dealing with cyclical unemployment?
card.a: If there is a recession and unemployment increases, we can call on an expansionary fiscal policy (lower taxes or increased government spending) or an expansionary monetary policy (increase the money supply and lower interest rates). Both policies stimulate output and decrease unemployment.

card.q: Explain how the natural rate of unemployment may be higher in low-income countries.
card.a: Aside from a high natural rate of unemployment due to government regulations, subsistence households may be counted as not working.

q: Which term matches this definition? “economy of a country that has demonstrated the ability to catch up to the technology leaders by investing in both physical and human capital”
why: converging economy: economy of a country that has demonstrated the ability to catch up to the technology leaders by investing in both physical and human capital

card.q: How does indexing wage contracts to inflation help workers?
card.a: Indexing wage contracts means wages rise when prices rise. This means what you can buy with your wages, your standard of living, remains the same. When wages are not indexed, or rise with inflation, your standard of living falls.

card.q: Use the AD/AS model to show how increases in government spending can lead to more inflation.
card.a: An increase in government spending shifts the AD curve to the right, raising both income and price levels.

card.q: Show, using the AD/AS model, how governments can use monetary policy to decrease the price level.
card.a: A decrease in the money supply will shift the AD curve leftward and reduce income and price levels. Banks will have less money to lend. Interest rates will increase, affecting consumption and investment, which are both key determinants of aggregate demand.

card.q: What do international flows of capital have to do with trade imbalances?
card.a: Given the high level of activity in international financial markets, it is typically believed that financial flows across borders are the real reason for trade imbalances. For example, the United States had an enormous trade deficit in the late 1990s and early 2000s because it was attracting vast inflows of foreign capital. Smaller countries that have attracted such inflows of international capital worry that if the inflows suddenly turn to outflows, the resulting decline in their currency could collapse their banking system and bring on a deep recession.

card.q: Use the demand-and-supply of foreign currency graph to determine what would happen to a small, open economy that experienced capital outflows.
card.a: The demand for the country’s currency would decrease, lowering the exchange rate.

q: Which term matches this definition? “when one country has more resources, more productive resources, or a natural endowment to produce a good compared to another country; when a country can produce more of a good compared to another country”
why: absolute advantage: when one country has more resources, more productive resources, or a natural endowment to produce a good compared to another country; when a country can produce more of a good compared to another country

q: Which term matches this definition? “a country that can consume more than it can produce as a result of specialization and trade”
why: gain from trade: a country that can consume more than it can produce as a result of specialization and trade

card.q: True or False: The source of comparative advantage must be natural elements like climate and mineral deposits. Explain.
card.a: False. Anything that leads to different levels of productivity between two economies can be a source of comparative advantage. For example, the education of workers, the knowledge base of engineers and scientists in a country, the part of a split-up value chain where they have their specialized learning, economies of scale, and other factors can all determine comparative advantage.

card.q: Brazil can produce 100 pounds of beef or 10 autos. In contrast the United States can produce 40 pounds of beef or 30 autos. Which country has the absolute advantage in beef? Which country has the absolute advantage in producing autos? What is the opportunity cost of producing one pound of beef in Brazil? What is the opportunity cost of producing one pound of beef in the United States?
card.a: Brazil has the absolute advantage in producing beef and the United States has the absolute advantage in autos. The opportunity cost of producing one pound of beef is 1/10 of an auto; in the United States it is 3/4 of an auto.

card.q: In France it takes one worker to produce one sweater, and one worker to produce one bottle of wine. In Tunisia it takes two workers to produce one sweater, and three workers to produce one bottle of wine. Who has the absolute advantage in production of sweaters? Who has the absolute advantage in the production of wine? How can you tell?
card.a: In answering questions like these, it is often helpful to begin by organizing the information in a table, such as in the following table. Notice that, in this case, the productivity of the countries is expressed in terms of how many workers it takes to produce a unit of a product. Country One Sweater One Bottle of wine France 1 worker 1 worker Tunisia 2 workers 3 workers In this example, France has an absolute advantage in the production of both sweaters and wine. You can tell because it takes France less labor to produce a unit of the good.

q: Which term matches this definition? “international trade of goods within the same industry”
why: intra-industry trade: international trade of goods within the same industry

q: Which term matches this definition? “many of the different stages of producing a good happen in different geographic locations”
why: splitting up the value chain: many of the different stages of producing a good happen in different geographic locations

q: Which term matches this definition? “how a good is produced in stages”
why: value chain: how a good is produced in stages

card.q: How can there be any economic gains for a country from both importing and exporting the same good, like cars?
card.a: There are a number of possible advantages of intra-industry trade. Both nations can take advantage of extreme specialization and learning in certain kinds of cars with certain traits, like gas-efficient cars, luxury cars, sport-utility vehicles, higher- and lower-quality cars, and so on. Moreover, nations can take advantage of economies of scale, so that large companies will compete against each other across international borders, providing the benefits of competition and variety to customers. This same argument applies to trade between U.S. states, where people often buy products made by people of other states, even though a similar product is made within the boundaries of their own state. All states—and all countries—can benefit from this kind of competition and trade.

q: Which term matches this definition? “taxes that governments place on imported goods”
why: tariffs: taxes that governments place on imported goods

card.q: If the removal of trade barriers is so beneficial to international economic growth, why would a nation continue to restrict trade on some imported or exported products?
card.a: A nation might restrict trade on imported products to protect an industry that is important for national security. For example, nation X and nation Y may be geopolitical rivals, each with ambitions of increased political and economic strength. Even if nation Y has comparative advantage in the production of missile defense systems, it is unlikely that nation Y would seek to export those goods to nation X. It is also the case that, for some nations, the production of a particular good is a key component of national identity. In Japan, the production of rice is culturally very important. It may be difficult for Japan to import rice from a nation like Vietnam, even if Vietnam has a comparative advantage in rice production.

q: Which term matches this definition? “numerical limits on the quantity of products that a country can import”
why: import quotas: numerical limits on the quantity of products that a country can import

q: Which term matches this definition? “ways a nation can draw up rules, regulations, inspections, and paperwork to make it more costly or difficult to import products”
options: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)
why: nontariff barriers: ways a nation can draw up rules, regulations, inspections, and paperwork to make it more costly or difficult to import products

q: Which term matches this definition? “government policies to reduce or block imports”
why: protectionism: government policies to reduce or block imports

q: Which term matches this definition? “organization that seeks to negotiate reductions in barriers to trade and to adjudicate complaints about violations of international trade policy; successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)”
options: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)
why: World Trade Organization (WTO): organization that seeks to negotiate reductions in barriers to trade and to adjudicate complaints about violations of international trade policy; successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)

card.q: Explain how a tariff reduction causes an increase in the equilibrium quantity of imports and a decrease in the equilibrium price. Hint: Consider the Work It Out "Effects of Trade Barriers."
card.a: This is the opposite case of the Work It Out feature. A reduced tariff is like a decrease in the cost of production, which is shown by a downward (or rightward) shift in the supply curve.

card.q: Explain how a subsidy on agricultural goods like sugar adversely affects the income of foreign producers of imported sugar.
card.a: A subsidy is like a reduction in cost. This shifts the supply curve down (or to the right), driving the price of sugar down. If the subsidy is large enough, the price of sugar can fall below the cost of production faced by foreign producers, which means they will lose money on any sugar they produce and sell.

card.q: Explain how trade barriers save jobs in protected industries, but only by costing jobs in other industries.
card.a: Trade barriers raise the price of goods in protected industries. If those products are inputs in other industries, it raises their production costs and then prices, so sales fall in those other industries. Lower sales lead to lower employment. Additionally, if the protected industries are consumer goods, their customers pay higher prices, which reduce demand for other consumer products and thus employment in those industries.

card.q: Explain how trade barriers raise wages in protected industries by reducing average wages economy-wide.
card.a: Trade based on comparative advantage raises the average wage rate economy-wide, though it can reduce the incomes of import-substituting industries. By moving away from a country’s comparative advantage, trade barriers do the opposite: they give workers in protected industries an advantage, while reducing the average wage economy-wide.

card.q: How does international trade affect working conditions of low-income countries?
card.a: By raising incomes, trade tends to raise working conditions also, even though those conditions may not (yet) be equivalent to those in high-income countries.

card.q: Do the jobs for workers in low-income countries that involve making products for export to high-income countries typically pay these workers more or less than their next-best alternative?
card.a: They typically pay more than the next-best alternative. If a Nike firm did not pay workers at least as much as they would earn, for example, in a subsistence rural lifestyle, they many never come to work for Nike.

card.q: How do trade barriers affect the average income level in an economy?
card.a: Since trade barriers raise prices, real incomes fall. The average worker would also earn less.

card.q: How does the cost of “saving” jobs in protected industries compare to the workers’ wages and salaries?
card.a: Workers working in other sectors and the protected sector see a decrease in their real wage.

q: Which term matches this definition? “laws that block imports sold below the cost of production and impose tariffs that would increase the price of these imports to reflect their cost of production”
why: anti-dumping laws: laws that block imports sold below the cost of production and impose tariffs that would increase the price of these imports to reflect their cost of production

q: Which term matches this definition? “selling internationally traded goods below their cost of production”
why: dumping: selling internationally traded goods below their cost of production

q: Which term matches this definition? “the argument that there are compelling national interests against depending on key imports from other nations”
why: national interest argument: the argument that there are compelling national interests against depending on key imports from other nations

q: Which term matches this definition? “when production locates in countries with the lowest environmental (or other) standards, putting pressure on all countries to reduce their environmental standards”
options: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)
why: race to the bottom: when production locates in countries with the lowest environmental (or other) standards, putting pressure on all countries to reduce their environmental standards

card.q: Explain how predatory pricing could be a motivation for dumping.
card.a: If imports can be sold at extremely low prices, domestic firms would have to match those prices to be competitive. By definition, matching prices would imply selling under cost and, therefore, losing money. Firms cannot sustain losses forever. When they leave the industry, importers can “take over,” raising prices to monopoly levels to cover their short-term losses and earn long-term profits.

card.q: Why do low-income countries like Brazil, Egypt, or Vietnam have lower environmental standards than high-income countries like the Germany, Japan, or the United States?
card.a: Because low-income countries need to provide necessities—food, clothing, and shelter—to their people. In other words, they consider environmental quality a luxury.

card.q: Explain the logic behind the “race to the bottom” argument and the likely reason it has not occurred.
card.a: Low-income countries can compete for jobs by reducing their environmental standards to attract business to their countries. This could lead to a competitive reduction in regulations, which would lead to greater environmental damage. While pollution management is a cost for businesses, it is tiny relative to other costs, like labor and adequate infrastructure. It is also costly for firms to locate far away from their customers, which many low-income countries are.

card.q: What are the conditions under which a country may use the unsafe products argument to block imports?
card.a: The decision should not be arbitrary or unnecessarily discriminatory. It should treat foreign companies the same way as domestic companies. It should be based on science.

card.q: Why is the national security argument not convincing?
card.a: Restricting imports today does not solve the problem. If anything, it makes it worse since it implies using up domestic sources of the products faster than if they are imported. Also, the national security argument can be used to support protection of nearly any product, not just things critical to our national security.

card.q: Assume a perfectly competitive market and the exporting country is small. Using a demand and supply diagram, show the impact of increasing standards on a low-income exporter of toys. Show the tariff's impact. Is the effect on toy prices the same or different? Why is a standards policy preferred to tariffs?
card.a: The effect of increasing standards may increase costs to the small exporting country. The supply curve of toys will shift to the left. Exports will decrease and toy prices will rise. Tariffs also raise prices. So the effect on the price of toys is the same. A tariff is a “second best” policy and also affects other sectors. However, a common standard across countries is a “first best” policy that attacks the problem at its root.

q: Which term matches this definition? “economic agreement between countries to allow free trade in goods, services, labor, and financial capital between members while having a common external trade policy”
options: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)
why: common market: economic agreement between countries to allow free trade in goods, services, labor, and financial capital between members while having a common external trade policy

q: Which term matches this definition? “economic agreement between countries to allow free trade between members, a common external trade policy, and coordinated monetary and fiscal policies”
options: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)
why: economic union: economic agreement between countries to allow free trade between members, a common external trade policy, and coordinated monetary and fiscal policies

q: Which term matches this definition? “economic agreement between countries to allow free trade between members”
why: free trade agreement: economic agreement between countries to allow free trade between members

q: Which term matches this definition? “forum in which nations could come together to negotiate reductions in tariffs and other barriers to trade; the precursor to the World Trade Organization”
options: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)
why: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT): forum in which nations could come together to negotiate reductions in tariffs and other barriers to trade; the precursor to the World Trade Organization

card.q: What is the difference between a free trade association, a common market, and an economic union?
card.a: A free trade association offers free trade between its members, but each country can determine its own trade policy outside the association. A common market requires a common external trade policy in addition to free trade within the group. An economic union is a common market with coordinated fiscal and monetary policy.

card.q: Why would countries promote protectionist laws, while also negotiate for freer trade internationally?
card.a: International agreements can serve as a political counterweight to domestic special interests, thereby preventing stronger protectionist measures.

card.q: What might account for the dramatic increase in international trade over the past 50 years?
card.a: Reductions in tariffs, quotas, and other trade barriers, improved transportation, and communication media have made people more aware of what is available in the rest of the world.

card.q: How does competition, whether domestic or foreign, harm businesses?
card.a: Competition from firms with better or cheaper products can reduce a business’s profits, and may drive it out of business. Workers would similarly lose income or even their jobs.

card.q: What are the gains from competition?
card.a: Consumers get better or less expensive products. Businesses with the better or cheaper products increase their profits. Employees of those businesses earn more income. On balance, the gains outweigh the losses to a nation.
